patient.chief_complaint: Witnessed generalized convulsive seizure preceded by recurrent episodes of an unusual taste and a rising sensation from the stomach
patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Kapoor is a 24-year-old right-handed South Asian female graduate student in biochemistry who was brought to the emergency department by her roommate after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure that occurred in their shared apartment this morning. Her roommate reports that the patient was sitting at her desk reading when she suddenly stopped and stared blankly ahead. She did not respond when her name was called. Her right hand began picking repetitively at the sleeve of her sweater, and she appeared to make chewing motions with her mouth. After approximately 25 seconds of this unresponsive behavior, she slid off the chair to the floor and developed bilateral limb stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking of all four extremities lasting approximately 60 to 70 seconds. The roommate called emergency services. Paramedics found the patient confused and unable to follow commands. On arrival to the emergency department approximately 40 minutes after the event, she was drowsy but arousable and increasingly coherent.

On interview, the patient reports that immediately before losing awareness she experienced an unusual metallic taste that she cannot otherwise characterize, accompanied by a rising warmth that started in her abdomen and moved upward into her chest. She felt briefly detached from her surroundings before the episode ended her memory. She has no recollection of anything until she found herself on the floor with paramedics present.

She reports that she has experienced similar episodes of the metallic taste with the rising abdominal sensation approximately six to eight times over the past ten months. These events have lasted 20 to 45 seconds and resolved spontaneously, leaving her mildly confused and fatigued. On two occasions, her roommate told her she appeared to be staring and unresponsive, and once seemed to be chewing and fidgeting with her hands, though the patient has no memory of these observations. She dismissed all episodes as stress or hypoglycemia related to long study hours and did not seek medical attention. She denies any prior history of unprovoked seizures, febrile convulsions, head trauma, encephalitis, or meningitis. She has had no recent illness, fever, or significant sleep deprivation beyond her usual graduate student schedule. Her last menstrual period was three weeks ago. She is not on any hormonal contraception. She takes loratadine occasionally but has not used it this week.

output.query: DNET dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor focal epilepsy antiepileptic drug treatment outcomes

results.title: Long-term epilepsy-associated tumors (LEATs): surgical outcomes and WHO 2021 classification
results.source: Blumcke I et al., Brain Pathology 2021;31(4):e12955
results.summary: DNETs are classified as WHO grade I glioneuronal tumors with negligible risk of malignant transformation. Gross total resection achieves seizure freedom (Engel class I) in 80-90% of cases. Medical management with AEDs may control seizures in a subset of patients prior to or instead of surgery.

results.title: Initial monotherapy for epileptic seizures: ILAE evidence-based guideline
results.summary: For focal-onset seizures, levetiracetam and lamotrigine have level A/B evidence as initial monotherapy in adults. Oxcarbazepine, carbamazepine, and lacosamide are also appropriate options. AED choice should account for patient age, sex, comorbidities, and drug interaction profile.

results.title: Focal epilepsy due to low-grade neuroepithelial tumors: natural history and medical management
results.summary: In patients with temporal lobe tumor-associated epilepsy, approximately 35-45% achieve meaningful seizure reduction with AEDs alone. Extended resection including mesial temporal structures may improve seizure outcomes when electrocorticography demonstrates epileptiform activity beyond lesion boundaries.

output.summary: DNETs are benign WHO grade I glioneuronal tumors. Initial AED therapy (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, or lacosamide as first-line for focal epilepsy) may reduce seizure burden prior to surgical evaluation. Gross total resection achieves seizure freedom in 80-90% of cases; AED monotherapy controls seizures in a subset. AED selection should be individualized to patient characteristics including sex and comedication profile.

interactions: No significant pharmacokinetic interaction with loratadine
Levetiracetam is non-enzyme-inducing and does not affect hormonal contraceptive efficacy if initiated in the future
warnings: Psychiatric adverse effects including irritability, anxiety exacerbation, and mood lability reported in approximately 10-15% of patients; monitor closely

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Focal epilepsy of left temporal lobe origin (dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor)

differential.key_features: Imaging cannot reliably distinguish DNET from ganglioglioma; tissue diagnosis required; both are benign, cortically based, and epileptogenic.

differential.diagnosis: Focal cortical dysplasia (type IIIb, associated with low-grade tumor)
differential.key_features: FCD may coexist with DNET at the lesion margin; concordant cortical location is consistent; histology clarifies.
Small lesion size and benign imaging appearance could prompt dismissal as incidental; however cortical location and concordance with EEG lateralization support epileptogenic role.
Left hippocampus is normal in volume and signal; the identified lesion is neocortical, not mesial.
Stereotyped mesial-temporal aura, concordant EEG, and structural lesion make PNES extremely unlikely.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed seizure history including semiology, aura character, automatisms, duration, frequency, witness accounts, and post-ictal features.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Stereotyped focal impaired-awareness events with left temporal-lobe aura (metallic taste, rising abdominal sensation) and post-ictal confusion.
Interictal exam typically normal; tongue bite on the right side consistent with contralateral motor manifestation of left temporal seizure.

optimal_actions.action: Order routine EEG to identify interictal epileptiform discharges and characterize the electrical seizure focus.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Frequent left anterior temporal spike-and-wave complexes (F7/T3) and left temporal TIRDA; no electrographic seizures on routine recording.

optimal_actions.action: Order MRI brain with dedicated epilepsy protocol (thin-cut coronal T1/FLAIR/T2/DWI through the hippocampi, with gadolinium).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Left anterior temporal cortically-based bubbly T2-hyperintense lesion without enhancement or edema — imaging features of a low-grade glioneuronal tumor (DNET or ganglioglioma).

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, prolactin (if within 10-20 minutes of seizure), and AED levels if on therapy.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Exclude metabolic provocation; elevated prolactin supports recent convulsive seizure; baseline organ function for AED selection.

optimal_actions.action: Search current literature for AED selection in focal epilepsy due to low-grade tumor and DNET management.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Evidence-based AED options for focal epilepsy (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, lacosamide); DNET surgical outcomes (Engel class I in 80-90% with gross total resection).

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating AED therapy, accounting for current medications and reproductive considerations.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Levetiracetam or lamotrigine have no significant interactions with loratadine and are non-enzyme-inducing; oxcarbazepine and carbamazepine are enzyme-inducing and would reduce hormonal contraceptive efficacy.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection, autoimmune encephalitis, or immunocompromise; LP is not indicated in routine focal epilepsy workup with an identified structural lesion and exposes the patient to unnecessary procedural risk.
No syncope-versus-seizure diagnostic question and no structural cardiac concern; echocardiogram contributes nothing to focal epilepsy workup.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is reserved for syncope-versus-seizure differentiation; semiology is clearly epileptic with a concordant structural lesion.
Head CT is inferior to dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI for detecting cortically-based low-grade lesions such as DNET and adds ionizing radiation without diagnostic yield.

sequence_constraints.reason: Identifying a cortically-based low-grade tumor informs AED selection — enzyme-inducing agents (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine) are preferentially avoided in young women of reproductive age who may require future surgical planning and hormonal contraception.

critical_actions: Recognize the metallic taste and rising abdominal sensation as left mesial/neocortical temporal aura; right-sided automatisms (right hand picking, right tongue bite) confirm left temporal onset.
Obtain MRI with epilepsy protocol to characterize the cortical lesion as a low-grade glioneuronal tumor concordant with the seizure focus.
Do not dismiss the small cortically-based left temporal lesion as an incidental finding — concordance with EEG lateralization establishes it as the epileptogenic substrate.
Initiate first-line AED for focal epilepsy (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, or lacosamide); avoid enzyme-inducing agents in a young woman of reproductive age.
Refer to epilepsy surgery program and neurosurgery for consideration of resection — DNET gross total resection achieves seizure freedom in 80-90% of cases.
Counsel on seizure precautions including driving restrictions and laboratory safety during graduate studies.
contraindicated_actions: Do not dismiss a small, benign-appearing cortically-based temporal lesion as non-epileptogenic when EEG lateralization is concordant.
Do not start enzyme-inducing AEDs (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin) without considering interactions with future hormonal contraception and surgical pharmacotherapy.
Do not perform lumbar puncture in the absence of features of CNS infection or autoimmune encephalitis.
key_reasoning_points: The combination of left anterior temporal spike-and-wave discharges on EEG and a concordant left temporal cortically-based bubbly T2-hyperintense non-enhancing lesion is the hallmark of DNET-associated focal epilepsy.
A small lesion size does not imply non-epileptogenicity — cortically-based DNETs are epileptogenic regardless of size when EEG focus is concordant.
Right-sided oroalimentary automatisms and right tongue bite are contralateral to the left temporal seizure onset, confirming left temporal localization by semiology.
DNET is a WHO grade I tumor; surgical resection offers the highest probability of seizure freedom and is preferred over lifelong AED therapy when the lesion is accessible.
In a young woman of reproductive age, non-enzyme-inducing AEDs (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, lacosamide) are preferred to preserve future contraceptive options and minimize teratogenic risk.

red_herrings.data_point: Left temporal DNET measuring only 14 x 11 x 10 mm (approximately 0.8 cm3) without mass effect, edema, or enhancement
red_herrings.intended_effect: A naive agent may interpret the small size and entirely benign imaging appearance of the lesion as evidence that it is a non-epileptogenic incidental developmental anomaly, and proceed to search for an alternative explanation for the seizures.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A cortically-based bubbly T2-hyperintense left temporal lesion without enhancement is the classical MRI appearance of DNET; small size and lack of mass effect are characteristic features, not evidence of non-epileptogenicity. Concordance with left anterior temporal EEG localizes this lesion as the epileptogenic substrate.
